visuals.title: Where sickle cell hits
visuals.text: Haemolysis, vaso-occlusion and infarction can damage almost any organ.

glossary.Haemoglobin: The oxygen-carrying protein inside red blood cells.
glossary.Sickling: Red cells deforming into a rigid crescent shape when HbS polymerises.
glossary.Vaso-occlusion: Blockage of small blood vessels, here by sickled red cells.
glossary.Anaemia: Low haemoglobin concentration in the blood.
glossary.Acidosis: Too much acid in the blood or tissues, a low pH.
glossary.Hypoxia: Too little oxygen reaching the tissues.
glossary.Prevalence: The proportion of a population who have a condition at a given time.
glossary.Sub-Saharan Africa: The part of Africa south of the Sahara desert, where the HbS gene is common.
glossary.Chronic haemolytic anaemia: Long-standing anaemia caused by ongoing early destruction of red cells.
glossary.Jaundice: Yellowing of skin and eyes from raised bilirubin.
glossary.Normocytic anaemia: Anaemia with normal-sized red cells (normal MCV).
glossary.Ischaemia: Inadequate blood supply to a tissue, starving it of oxygen.
glossary.Infarction: Tissue death caused by loss of its blood supply.
glossary.Hand-foot syndrome: Painful swelling of the hands and feet from bone infarction in young children; another name for dactylitis.
glossary.Consolidation: Lung air spaces filled with fluid, pus or cells, so they appear solid on X-ray.
glossary.Bronchial breathing: Harsh, hollow breath sounds heard over consolidated lung.
glossary.Crackles: Fine clicking sounds on auscultation as fluid-filled airways open.
glossary.Pulmonary infiltrates: Hazy shadowing on chest X-ray from fluid, cells or inflammation in the lung.
glossary.Splenic infarction: Death of spleen tissue from blocked blood supply.
glossary.Streptococcus pneumoniae: Pneumococcus: an encapsulated bacterium causing pneumonia, meningitis and sepsis.
glossary.Haemophilus influenzae: Encapsulated bacterium causing chest infections, meningitis and epiglottitis.
glossary.Neisseria meningitidis: Meningococcus: encapsulated bacterium causing meningitis and septicaemia.
glossary.Pseudomonas aeruginosa: Gram-negative bacterium that infects vulnerable or immunocompromised patients.
glossary.Shock: Inadequate blood flow to organs, causing tissue hypoxia.
glossary.E. coli O157: A toxin-producing strain of E. coli that can trigger haemolysis and kidney injury.
glossary.Stroke: Sudden brain damage from blocked or bleeding blood vessels.
glossary.FBC: Full blood count: haemoglobin, white cells, platelets and red cell indices.
glossary.MRI: Magnetic resonance imaging, a scan that shows soft tissue and bone marrow in detail.
glossary.Rehydration: Replacing lost body water by mouth or drip.
glossary.IV fluids: Fluids given directly into a vein.
glossary.Transfusion: Giving donated blood or blood components.
glossary.SpO2: Oxygen saturation measured by a pulse oximeter.
glossary.Respiratory distress: Visible struggle to breathe: fast breathing, accessory muscle use, recession.
glossary.Multi-organ failure: Failure of two or more organ systems at once.
glossary.Prophylactic: Given to prevent disease rather than treat it.
glossary.Folic acid: B vitamin needed to make new red cells; replaces stores used up by high red cell turnover.
glossary.Beta-globin: One of the protein chains making up adult haemoglobin; mutated in sickle cell disease.
glossary.Point mutation: A change in a single DNA base.
glossary.Viscosity: Thickness or stickiness of a fluid, here blood.
glossary.Premature haemolysis: Red cells destroyed before their normal 120-day lifespan.
glossary.Chronic kidney disease: Long-term reduction in kidney function lasting over 3 months.
glossary.Reticulocytosis: Raised number of young red cells, showing the marrow is working harder.
glossary.Fetal haemoglobin: HbF, the haemoglobin made before birth; it does not sickle.
glossary.Asplenia: Absence or loss of function of the spleen.
